title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.
checks.explanation: The abstract places the gene at 10q24. The narrower band 10q24.2 is standard gene-location nomenclature, so it counts as restating the paper.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its features are an abnormal, 'inverted' facial expression, in which patients grimace or appear to be crying when they try to smile, together with urinary tract disease (Wang et al., 1997; Derbent et al., 2009). The bladder fails to empty completely even though there is no anatomical bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurological damage (Daly et al., 2010). Patients present with enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction caused by neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). Reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract puts the kidneys at risk, and some severely affected patients develop hypertension and progress to end-stage renal disease (Derbent et al., 2009; Daly et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families. In one family the parents were first cousins. The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. They also had urinary tract abnormalities: hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal urethral caliber in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and a trabeculated bladder with diverticula and severe mucosal hypertrophy with sclerotic changes.

paragraphs.text: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) reported 36 children, seen between 1965 and 1986, who had enuresis and urinary tract infection along with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic workup found mild neuropathic bladder in every case, and most patients had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) reported 3 European patients with urofacial syndrome. They noted that the condition was originally described in Colombian patients and has rarely been reported from other countries. They suggested that cases may be missed because the urinary problems vary and the characteristic facial grimacing goes unrecognized.

paragraphs.text: In contrast, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) concluded that urofacial syndrome is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Their evidence was multiple affected sibs, unaffected parents, an increased rate of parental consanguinity, and an equal sex ratio. Later reports also described the disorder as autosomal recessive (Wang et al., 1997; Daly et al., 2010). Daly et al. (2010) found homozygous mutations in the HPSE2 gene in affected families.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) carried out a genome screen that combined homozygosity mapping with DNA pooling. The study used 20 selected UFS patients, one patient pool, and three control pools of unaffected relatives. Of 36 randomly chosen markers, D10S677 showed linkage to and association with UFS. Patients had a significant excess of homozygosity at this marker compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)), and allele frequencies differed between patient and control pools. The authors then typed 10 more markers spanning 22 cM around D10S677 for haplotype (linkage disequilibrium) analysis. All 31 patients were homozygous for D10S1726 and D10S198, which lie about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, compared with 12% of unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinations in several patients who were heterozygous at the flanking markers D10S1433 (centromeric) and D10S603 (telomeric) placed the UFS gene in a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Because 'inversion' of facial expression is clearly linked to neuropathic bladder and the resulting damage to the genitourinary tract, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) recommended urologic evaluation for anyone with this facial sign.

checks.evidence_quote: The clear association of distortion in facial expression and neuropathic bladder with resultant damage to the genitourinary tract
checks.explanation: Restates the association described in the paper.

checks.claim: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) recommended urologic evaluation for anyone with 'inversion' of facial expression.
checks.evidence_quote: should prompt urological evaluation of individuals with "inversion" of facial expression.
checks.explanation: The authors recommend urologic evaluation for people with this facial sign.

paragraphs.text: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stressed that early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of the urinary problems. Aydogdu et al. (2010) made the same point about urinary problems caused by a dysfunctional bladder. Derbent et al. (2009) noted that the diagnosis can be missed because the urinary problems vary and the facial grimacing goes unrecognized. They recommended that physicians consider urofacial syndrome in any patient with dysfunctional voiding, especially in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.

checks.claim: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stressed that early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome has important consequences for the management and prognosis of the urinary problems.
checks.evidence_quote: Establishing an early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of urinary problems in these patients.

checks.claim: Aydogdu et al. (2010) stressed that early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome has important consequences for the management and prognosis of urinary problems caused by a dysfunctional bladder.
checks.evidence_quote: Early diagnosis is crucial for the management and prognosis of urinary problems due to a dysfunctional bladder.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this point directly.

checks.claim: Derbent et al. (2009) noted that the diagnosis of urofacial syndrome can be missed because the urinary problems vary and the facial grimacing goes unrecognized.
checks.evidence_quote: the diagnosis may be missed because of variability of these problems and failure to recognize the characteristic facial grimacing

checks.claim: Derbent et al. (2009) recommended that physicians consider urofacial syndrome in any patient with dysfunctional voiding, especially in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.
checks.evidence_quote: Physicians should keep this syndrome in mind for any patient who presents with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Abnormal facial expression ('inverted' smile; grimacing when attempting to smile)

paragraphs.text: Daly et al. (2010) used whole-genome SNP mapping to define a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24 in an individual with urofacial syndrome. Within this region they identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) used whole-genome SNP mapping to define a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24 in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24

checks.claim: Within the 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24, Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified
